decks.title: Nutrition — Part 1: Classes of food, minerals and vitamins
goals: State the functions and common sources of carbohydrates, fats, proteins and water
State the function of calcium, iodine, iron and sodium and the effect of their deficiency
Match each vitamin with its source, function and deficiency disease

slides.heading: Food and Nutrition
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what our food is made of, and what each part does for the body.

visual.alt: Flow from food to the main food classes and to mineral salts and vitamins

slides.narration: Food gives the body energy, materials to grow and repair, and substances that keep it working well. Biologists group food into classes, and each class has its own jobs.

slides.heading: Carbohydrates, fats, proteins and water

rows: Store of energy; keep the body warm; protect organs; carry some vitamins
Growth and repair of cells; make enzymes and antibodies
Solvent for substances; carries them around the body; cools the body by sweat

visual.alt: Table of the functions and sources of carbohydrates, fats, proteins and water

slides.narration: Carbohydrates are the main energy food. Fats store energy and keep the body warm. Proteins build and repair the body. Water dissolves substances, carries them around the body, and cools us down when we sweat.

slides.heading: Energy from a meal
slides.body_md: One gram of **fat** gives about **thirty-seven** kilojoules; one gram of **carbohydrate** or **protein** gives about **seventeen**.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: energy in a breakfast
slides.body_md: A breakfast has 60 g of carbohydrate, 15 g of protein and 10 g of fat. Using 17 kJ per g for carbohydrate and protein and 37 kJ per g for fat, find the total energy and the percentage from fat.
bullets: Step 1: carbohydrate = 60 × 17 = **1020 kJ**; protein = 15 × 17 = **255 kJ**; fat = 10 × 37 = **370 kJ**.
Step 3: fat share = 370 ÷ 1645 × 100 = **22.5 percent**.

visual.alt: Worked table of the energy in a breakfast by food class and in total

slides.narration: Multiply the grams of each class by its energy per gram. Add the three results to get sixteen hundred and forty five kilojoules. Then divide the energy from fat by the total and multiply by one hundred to get twenty two point five percent.

slides.heading: Quick check: the energy food
slides.body_md: Which class of food is the main source of energy in the diet?
slides.narration: Think of rice and wheat.

slides.heading: Mineral salts

rows: Builds bones and teeth; helps blood to clot; muscle action
Weak bones and teeth; rickets in children
Milk, cheese, ragi, green leafy vegetables
Needed to make thyroxine in the thyroid gland
Makes haemoglobin of red blood cells
Nerve messages; water balance; muscle action

visual.alt: Table of calcium, iodine, iron and sodium with function, deficiency and sources

slides.narration: Minerals are needed in small amounts. Calcium builds bones and teeth. Iodine is needed for the thyroid gland. Iron makes haemoglobin, so lack of it causes anaemia. Sodium helps nerves and muscles.

slides.heading: Where minerals are needed
slides.body_md: **Iodine** works in the **thyroid**, **iron** in the **blood**, **sodium** in **nerves and muscles**, and **calcium** in **bones and teeth**.

slides.narration: Here is where each mineral does its main work. Iodine is used in the thyroid gland of the neck. Iron is part of haemoglobin in blood. Sodium is used in nerves and muscles. Calcium builds the teeth and bones.

slides.heading: Quick check: a swollen neck
slides.body_md: Deficiency of which mineral causes goitre?
slides.narration: The thyroid gland needs it.

slides.heading: Vitamins

rows: Releases energy from carbohydrates; healthy nerves
Healthy gums and skin; heals wounds
Sunlight, egg yolk, fish liver oil
Bleeding that is slow to stop

visual.alt: Table of vitamins A, B1, C, D and K with function, deficiency disease and sources

slides.narration: Vitamins are needed in very small amounts, but each has a clear job. Vitamin A for the eyes, vitamin B one for energy release and nerves, vitamin C for gums and skin, vitamin D for bones, and vitamin K for blood clotting.

slides.heading: Quick check: bleeding gums
slides.narration: Think of citrus fruits.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: a clinic survey
slides.body_md: A clinic sees 60 patients with a vitamin deficiency: 12 lack vitamin A, 9 lack B1, 15 lack C, 18 lack D and 6 lack K. What percentage lack vitamin D? How many lack a water-soluble vitamin (B1 or C)?
bullets: Step 1: percentage lacking D = 18 ÷ 60 × 100 = **30 percent**.
Step 2: water-soluble = B1 + C = 9 + 15 = **24**.
Step 3: the other **36** lack a fat-soluble vitamin (A, D or K).

visual.alt: Worked table of sixty clinic patients by the vitamin they lack and whether it is fat-soluble or water-soluble

slides.narration: Divide the number lacking vitamin D by sixty and multiply by one hundred, which gives thirty percent. Vitamins B and C dissolve in water, so add fifteen and nine to find twenty four patients. The rest lack a fat soluble vitamin.

slides.heading: Quick check: bones and sunlight
slides.body_md: A child with bow legs probably lacks which vitamin?
slides.narration: The skin makes it in sunlight.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Carbohydrates give energy; fats store it; proteins build and repair; water carries and cools.
Calcium: bones. Iodine: thyroid. Iron: blood. Sodium: nerves and muscles.
Vitamin A: night blindness. B1: beri-beri. C: scurvy. D: rickets. K: slow clotting.
Vitamins A, D and K are fat-soluble; B and C are water-soluble.

visual.alt: Summary table of five deficiencies and their effects

slides.narration: To recap. Learn the job of each food class, and match each mineral and vitamin with its deficiency disease. Iodine and goitre, iron and anaemia, vitamin C and scurvy, vitamin D and rickets, and vitamin A and night blindness.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **function**, **source** and **deficiency** when a question asks about a mineral or vitamin.
Do not mix **scurvy** (vitamin C) with **rickets** (vitamin D).
Write **goitre** for iodine and **anaemia** for iron.
Show **units** and **steps** in an energy calculation.
slides.narration: Exam tips. For a mineral or vitamin, give its function, a source and the deficiency disease. Do not mix up scurvy and rickets. Remember goitre for iodine and anaemia for iron. In an energy sum, show each step.

goals: Explain the meaning and importance of a balanced diet
Explain why cellulose is useful in the diet though humans cannot digest it

slides.heading: Eating Well
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the balanced diet, the role of roughage, and what happens when the diet fails.

visual.alt: Flow from the balanced diet to roughage and to malnutrition

slides.narration: A healthy body needs the right food in the right amounts. We look at what a balanced diet means, why plant fibre matters, and what goes wrong when children do not get enough food or the right food.

slides.heading: A balanced diet

rows: A diet that has all the food classes, minerals, vitamins, water and roughage, in the right amounts
Age, sex, body size, occupation and health
A growing child needs more protein; a heavy labourer needs more energy foods
Gives energy and growth, prevents deficiency diseases, keeps the body healthy

visual.alt: Table giving the meaning of a balanced diet, what decides it and why it is important

slides.narration: A balanced diet contains all the nutrients in the right amounts for the person. A growing child, a heavy labourer and an elderly person need different amounts. A balanced diet prevents deficiency diseases.

slides.heading: A plate for a balanced diet
slides.body_md: A plate model: **cereals** take the biggest share, with **pulses, vegetables and fruits, milk** and a little **oil**.

slides.heading: Roughage: the role of cellulose

rows: Cellulose: the fibre in plant cell walls
No: we do not make the enzyme that breaks it down
Adds bulk to the food waste; holds water; helps the gut muscles to push food on
Vegetables, fruits with peel, whole grains, pulses

visual.alt: Table about cellulose: what it is, why it is not digested, why it is useful, the effect of too little and sources

slides.narration: Cellulose is the fibre in plant food. We cannot digest it, but it is still useful. It adds bulk, holds water, and helps the gut push food along, so it prevents constipation.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: fibre in the diet
slides.body_md: A person eats 300 g of vegetables a day, with 3 g of fibre in every 100 g. The daily target is 30 g. How much fibre does the person get, and how much more is needed?
bullets: Step 1: fibre from vegetables = 300 ÷ 100 × 3 = **9 g**.
Step 2: still needed = 30 − 9 = **21 g**.
Step 3: the vegetables give 9 ÷ 30 × 100 = **30 percent** of the target; add whole grains, pulses and fruit.

visual.alt: Worked table of the fibre target, the fibre from vegetables and the fibre still needed

slides.narration: Three hundred grams of vegetables is three lots of one hundred, so nine grams of fibre. The target is thirty grams, so twenty one grams more are needed. The person should add whole grains, pulses and fruit.

sections.heading: 1. Classes of food: carbohydrates, fats, proteins and water
sections.body_md:
| Class | Functions | Common sources |
|---|---|---|
| **Carbohydrates** | Main source of **energy** (about 17 kJ per g) | Rice, wheat, potato, sugar, fruits |
| **Fats** | **Store** of energy (about 37 kJ per g); keep the body **warm** (insulation); **protect** organs; carry **fat-soluble vitamins** | Oil, ghee, butter, nuts |
| **Proteins** | **Growth and repair** of cells; make **enzymes**, hormones and antibodies; can give energy (about 17 kJ per g) | Pulses, milk, eggs, fish, meat |
| **Water** (about 70 percent of the body mass) | **Solvent**; **carries** nutrients, gases and wastes; **cools** the body by sweat; needed for chemical reactions | Drinks, fruits, vegetables |

Energy values are approximate (books also use 4, 4 and 9 kilocalories per gram). **Weight for weight, fat gives a little more than twice the energy of carbohydrate.**

sections.heading: 3. Vitamins: sources, functions and deficiency diseases
sections.body_md:
| Vitamin | Function | Deficiency disease | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | Healthy eyes and skin | **Night blindness**; dry eyes | Carrot, papaya, milk, liver, fish liver oil |
| **B1** (thiamine) | Releases energy from carbohydrates; healthy nerves | **Beri-beri** | Whole grains, pulses, yeast, unpolished rice |
| **C** | Healthy gums and skin; heals wounds | **Scurvy** (bleeding gums) | Amla, orange, lemon, guava |
| **D** | Helps absorb **calcium and phosphorus** for bones | **Rickets** in children (bow legs) | Sunlight on the skin, egg yolk, fish liver oil |
| **K** | Helps blood to **clot** | Bleeding that is slow to stop | Green vegetables |

**Vitamins A, D, E and K** are **fat-soluble**; **B and C** are **water-soluble**. Vitamin E (protects cells; some books link it to fertility) is not asked in detail. Cooking can destroy vitamin C.

key_terms.definition_md: An organic substance needed in tiny amounts to keep the body healthy.
A vitamin that dissolves in fat: A, D, E and K.
A disease caused by a long-term lack of a nutrient.

sections.heading: 4. Balanced diet and the role of cellulose (roughage)
sections.body_md:
A **balanced diet** contains **all the food classes, mineral salts, vitamins, water and roughage in the right amounts**. The amounts depend on **age, sex, body size, occupation and state of health**: a growing child needs more protein, a heavy labourer more energy foods. It supplies energy, allows growth and repair, and prevents deficiency diseases.

**Cellulose** is the fibre of plant cell walls. Humans **cannot digest** it, because they do not make the enzyme that breaks it down. It is still useful as **roughage**: it adds **bulk** to the food waste, holds **water**, and helps the muscles of the gut to push the food on, so it **prevents constipation**. Sources: vegetables, fruits with peel, whole grains, pulses.

**Plate model:** a plate with cereals (largest share), pulses/eggs/fish, vegetables and fruits, milk and a little oil is one simple picture; the shares in the figure are illustrative and books differ.

key_terms.definition_md: A diet with all nutrients, water and roughage in the amounts the person needs.
Indigestible plant fibre, mainly cellulose, that adds bulk to the diet.
The carbohydrate of plant cell walls, not digested by humans.

sections.heading: 5. Malnutrition: kwashiorkor and marasmus
sections.body_md:
**Malnutrition** is a condition caused by a diet that is lacking in, or has too much of, one or more nutrients.

| Feature | Kwashiorkor | Marasmus |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Too little **protein** (diet mostly starchy foods); energy may be enough | Too little food of **all kinds**: lack of **energy and protein** |
| Usual age | Young children, about **1 to 5 years**, often after weaning | **Infants** under one year |
| Belly and limbs | **Swollen belly** (fluid, oedema); **thin** limbs | **No swelling**; very **thin, wasted** body |
| Face and hair | Puffy face; pale, thin hair; skin sores | **Shrunken, old-looking** face; ribs show |
| Behaviour | Irritable, listless | Weak, hungry, cries little |

**Prevention:** breast-feeding of infants; protein-rich weaning foods (pulses, milk, eggs); a balanced diet for the family; clean water, vaccination and treatment of infections; health education.

key_terms.definition_md: Ill-health caused by a diet that lacks or has too much of a nutrient.
Severe protein deficiency in young children, with a swollen belly.
Severe deficiency of food, energy and protein, in infants, with a wasted body.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Mixing up **scurvy** (vitamin C) and **rickets** (vitamin D), or **goitre** (iodine) and **anaemia** (iron).
- Giving a function without a **deficiency disease** and a **source**.
- Writing that fat gives "nine" or "thirty-seven" without the unit or the "per gram".
- Writing that cellulose is digested, or that roughage "gives energy".
- Calling marasmus a protein-only deficiency, or kwashiorkor a lack of all food.
- Forgetting that a balanced diet **depends on the person** (age, work).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, a deficiency disease, an odd one out **with its category**, a reason.
- 2 marks: two functions, or two differences matched point for point.
- 3 marks: a table of three differences, or three points with an example.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is usually a labelled diagram or a graph.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: we should drink more water in hot weather.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of water in the human body.

questions.solution_md: False. Humans cannot digest cellulose; it only adds roughage.

answer.model_answer_md: The cellulose acts as **roughage**: it adds **bulk** to the food waste and **prevents constipation**.

questions.stem_md: A person eats 300 g of vegetables with 3 g of fibre in each 100 g. The target is 30 g of fibre a day. How many more grams of fibre are needed?
questions.solution_md: Fibre eaten $= 300 \div 100 \times 3 = 9$ g; still needed $= 30 - 9 = 21$ g.

questions.stem_md: What is a balanced diet? Name one factor on which the amounts of food needed depend.

answer.model_answer_md: A **balanced diet** has **all the nutrients, water and roughage in the amounts the person needs**. The amounts depend on the person's **age** (or sex, size, occupation or health).

questions.solution_md: All nutrients in right amounts; one factor.

questions.stem_md: Why is cellulose useful in the diet although humans cannot digest it?

answer.model_answer_md: Cellulose forms **roughage**: it adds **bulk** to the food waste and holds water, helping the gut to push it on, and so **prevents constipation**. We cannot digest it because we **lack the enzyme** that breaks it down.

questions.solution_md: Roughage adds bulk; prevents constipation.

questions.stem_md: State three reasons why a balanced diet is important.

1. It supplies enough **energy** for work, play and growth, according to the needs of the person.
2. It supplies proteins and minerals as materials for **growth and repair** of the body.
3. It supplies vitamins and minerals in the right amounts, so it **prevents deficiency diseases** and keeps the body healthy.

questions.solution_md: Energy; growth and repair; prevents deficiency diseases.

questions.stem_md:
A nutritionist plans meals for a college hostel. One student eats 300 g of vegetables a day, with 3 g of fibre in each 100 g. The daily target is 30 g of fibre.

(a) Define a balanced diet. [2]

(b) Explain why cellulose cannot be digested by humans and why it is still useful. [3]

(c) Calculate the fibre from the vegetables and the fibre still needed. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a plate showing five food groups for a balanced diet. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A **balanced diet** contains **all the nutrients, water and roughage in the amounts the person needs**, according to age, sex, size, occupation and health.

**(b)** Humans **lack the enzyme** that breaks cellulose down. It is useful as **roughage**: it adds **bulk**, holds water and helps the gut to push the food on, so it **prevents constipation**.

**(c)** Fibre eaten = 300 ÷ 100 × 3 = **9 g**; still needed = 30 − 9 = **21 g**.

**(d)** A circle in five sectors: **cereals** (largest), **pulses, eggs and fish**, **vegetables and fruits**, **milk** and **oil**. Five labels.

questions.solution_md: All nutrients in right amounts; no enzyme, adds bulk; 9 g and 21 g; labelled plate.

(a) Calculate the mass of water in the body of the student. [2]
